newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek socialist PM wins election gamble.
newsitem.headline: Greek socialist PM wins election gamble.

text.p: Greece's socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis won his first major political gamble on Sunday, sweeping to victory in early national elections.
After stumbling in his first national campaign, Simitis, 60, showed he was a quick learner by changing his tactics and coming back strong at the finish.
His win marked the end of a long wait in Greece's political wilderness and then a meteoric rise to power in the past eight months.
It gave him complete control over the Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK), a free hand to name a cabinet of his choosing and a four-year mandate to implement his reform policies.
An enigma to many, he was dubbed "the Chinese" by the media for his slight build, almond-shaped eyes and inscrutible grin.
"I support him. I don't know why. I just think he's the only way forward for the party and the country but I can't give you a concrete reason. It's a feeling," a former PASOK official said.
A German and British-trained economist, Simitis emerged from the socialist shadows after party founder and three-time premier Andreas Papandreou was taken ill in January.
With lightning moves, he won a fight in the parliamentary group to replace Papandreou as premier. He then won the PASOK leadership in a close race after Papandreou died in June.
Unpretentious but supremely self-confident, Simitis had long seen himself as the only obvious heir-apparent to Papandreou, the one-time mentor with whom he had tense relations.
Papandreou named him to every cabinet but never included him in his inner circle and Simitis twice resigned from ministries because of public humiliations by the revered party founder.
In the end those disputes with Papandreou gave him the image of being his own man, and enhanced his popularity with the PASOK rank-and-file when the time came to choose an heir.
Simitis disliked Papandreou's flamboyant style and appeal to radical populism in formulating policy, which alienated allies and left Greece weakened internationally.
His own style is dry, even tedious, and in contrast to the extrovert and fun-loving Papandreou. He is a private man who prefers to stay home with a good book.

He billed himself the face of change for the 21st century but steered clear of giving details. Instead he catered to lofty dialogues on the EU, the need to work and sacrifice, and visions of Greece's potential as a Balkan and Mediterranean leader.
Simitis will give the first indication of just how different his "new PASOK" will be on Tuesday when he is likely to name his cabinet.
He is the son of a Piraeus lawyer and grew up in a well-off, progressive family, where the first seeds of his leftist views were sown.
He left home at 18 to study law and economics in Germany and did post-graduate work at the London School of Economics. He has worked as a lawyer and taught law and economics in Germany.
Simitis opposed a military junta which seized power in 1967 and was a founding member of Papandreou's PASOK when the regime fell in 1974.
During the junta Simitis escaped to Germany on a false passport while his wife was arrested and put in isolation. He was convicted in absentia for his opposition to the dictators.
